utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: His microphone is obviously not on. His microphones are now on. Are you able to hear through the earphones, usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do hear it, but there are noises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I can hear very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you described the beatings that you heard over a couple of months. When you heard these beatings, how long did they last usually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could well last between half an hour to an hour, sometimes longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the beatings stopped, could you hear anything else, or did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that because we followed it. And after that, we would always hear a car engine being switched on and that car leaving, and at some point we would think as if we'd heard -- as if I've heard that something was being thrown into water, or that was the assumption in the view of the time elapsed between the ignition of the engine and the place on the bridge that I know and from which something -- people could be thrown into the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was the noise level, the general noise level in the KP Dom or around the KP Dom at night when you heard that? Could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was by and large in the evening hours, that is after nine or ten, that is, 21 or 2200. It was a quiet night. One could hear everything, even a fly fly by or a cat walk by. I think one could recognise it, so that we could easily identify sounds. I said sounds of a car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the sounds or the noise of the river? Is the river loud? Can you hear the river very loud?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right now I don't remember, but from the river you hear, you know, the sound of something falling into the river, that kind of a sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear shots in relation to the beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was once they heard shots in the evening. On one occasion I heard shots in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe when you heard the shots? Was it after the beating had stopped, or was it while you still heard beating sounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When everything quieted down in those rooms where they were beaten, after that. It was after that that I heard shots on one occasion, and I heard beatings several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall which detainees had been taken on that occasion when you heard the beating -- the sound, the shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the Schedule C, that is, P55.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you have already mentioned several detainees you remembered in particular. Would you please now go with me through this list in front of you and tell us whom of these detainees you knew and what happened to them. Do you know number one, Alija Altoka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name does ring a bell, Alija, but I can't recall the features of the man. I can't remember the face. I don't remember what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second one, Salem Bico, do you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. I knew Salem Bico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see him in the, in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him in KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him? Did you see anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing particular. I know he was there, and I know he never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he taken out for these sort of beatings you saw, you have described to us, or did he disappear otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person number 3, Abdurahman Cankusic, do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know him personally, but his name I know. And I know that he was in the KP Dom, but I know nothing personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next person, number 4, Refik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same thing as Abdurahman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 5?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the KP Dom and can you tell us what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in the KP Dom and I do not know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Juso Dzamalija, person number 6?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him personally, but I did hear that he hanged himself, Juso Dzamalija, that he hanged himself. We heard it while in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 7, did you know him personally and can you tell us what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Kemal Dzelilovic and I saw him in the KP Dom. I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next person, number 8, Ramo Dzendusic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him too, but again I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 9, Adil Granov?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Adil Granov too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to him? Did you see anything about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I heard both about him, about the previous one, about Adil, that they were beaten overnight and they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that? How did you hear it? From other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From other detainees because we had a system of communication; we could exchange information with other rooms. These were not in my room, so that I cannot really say anything. I cannot say that I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned number 10, Nail Hodzic. If you yourself look through the list, can you pick from the list people who were in your room and that you saw what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned Zulfo Veiz, 29, and Enes Uzunovic. Adil Krajein was also in my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's number 14. What did you see happen to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when they took him out. They only took out Adil Krajein. He walked on his own two feet, but he never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was taken, did you hear the sounds of beating afterwards? Is he one of those who was taken out for beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly whether he was beaten. No, I can't. I can't really say because I did not see it, I did not hear, but he did not return to the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he taken in that period of beatings or was he taken later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else that we have not yet mentioned yesterday from the list where you actually saw or heard something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed, or rather I saw, when Nail Hodzic and three others whom I did not know -- I do not know those three. It could be one of those, but I simply do not know them. Three other men with Nail Hodzic went and were beaten, but I do not know who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And anyone else from the list, from your room, that you see or are these the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put the list aside. You have already mentioned that some detainees were released and others were exchanged. How many -- can you estimate how many detainees were exchanged, and did you actually see them later on, meet them somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I learned subsequently, that is, after I was released, I subsequently learned that about 300, 350 people disappeared. I saw very few people again, that is, those who were reportedly exchanged. Some may have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned already this person Halid Konjo and you said that he was exchanged and that he then disappeared. Do you recall, when he was taken from the KP Dom, was he taken alone or in a group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken with a group of people. I think it was September or October. He was not in my room. But at that time we were already freer, we could communicate better. And he went with a group to allegedly pick plums. I wanted also to volunteer to go there, but I was in a different room, and the guard would not allow me to go there because I wasn't envisaged for that job. And from my room, and I was in room 21 at the time, some 15 to 20 young men left and did not come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did guards ever mention the fate of these detainees, or maybe someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, to a guard, Vlatko Pljevaljcic -- yes, Pljevaljcic, he called me out in the evening at 11.00 to look at some gadget that he had. And I asked him, "Well, where are those people? Why aren't they coming back?" And they told me that they had gone to Bileca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone else mention something in relation to this particular group of let's call them plum pickers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once investigator Koprivica wanted to talk to me because I had asked to be received by him, and I asked him too what had happened with those men who had left, and his only answer was, "Don't ask me that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself ever taken for an exchange and then returned to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In July we were taken for exchange to a place called Cajnice, and we were about 25 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they came to fetch us, and we left in a lorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who selected you, your group of people? Who of the prison staff was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the investigator Koprivica, and he told me that he had picked me out. And then judging by the structure of those who left, it seemed that they had all been picked out, selected. One of the colleagues who was with me told me that he had been picked out by Warden Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who? Who did tell you? Do you know the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A prison -- an inmate. He is on the list of the protected ones, so I would rather not mention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the number of this person, if you have the number of this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see him here. I don't see him here, but I do think -- I'm afraid that this might be a mistake. I can write it down, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can the witness have a sheet of paper to write the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd better have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd better have a look at it so you see the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, there is, but I don't have the number right now. I would have to check. Your Honour, I think that's actually the witness we want to summons. That is the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, he has a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, he is not our witness yet. He doesn't have a number, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's something we can give him right now. This is the one that both parties want to call?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, what's the next number in the FWS series, or could we give him some initials? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think it would be best to give him initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, his pseudonym will be RJ, so Witness RJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This document we will make an exhibit, P407, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned you have written down the name of this person that we will call now RJ, and would you please tell us what he told you and when did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when we had reached the first stop near Cajnice, a school there, and when we looked around, we saw that, again, this was a company which had been picked out individually; it wasn't just random. And that is why the investigator Koprivica who saw me off and say good-bye, and then there were some other friends of mine, unfortunately I have to say that they are gone, they're missing. There was (redacted), a painter. There was Karabegovic, Pasovic. We were all -- we all socialised with investigator Koprivica, and we assumed that he had already sent them, like me, for exchange. But in addition to RJ, there were those we guessed that had been picked out for exchange by Warden Krnojelac; that is, we talked among ourselves and we made various assumptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. RJ tell you that it was his assumption, or did he even know that Mr. Krnojelac had selected him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: RJ was mentioned, his name came up on various occasions while in the KP Dom because Warden Krnojelac received him right before the exchange. He again went to see Warden Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I would like to know from you is, did Mr. RJ himself tell you that it was his assumption, or was it just you and the other detainees' assumption?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From RJ himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that RJ was not the only one that you thought Mr. Krnojelac had picked for this exchange. How many did he -- what was the assumption in relation to that? Who else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention also FWS-86. I can also mention yet another one, but from what I know, the same holds true of him as of RJ, and he was also with us when we went for that exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And when you were in Cajnice, did other people from other places when in Foca arrive there as well for the exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Cajnice, we were told that there were not enough people and that they were looking for more people to be exchanged, and then we spent the night there, waiting for others to come. In that other group there were a couple of elderly men, mostly women, young women and women of a certain age. There could have been some 15 of them. And there were some who seemed to have been wounded who needed medical care, and I saw a doctor come and extend aid to them. So that we were up to 40, perhaps 45 in Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These other persons, these women and elderly, where did they come from; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were together in that room, and they told us what they had gone through. They had been in a different camp which was called -- female, a women's camp in Foca in the building of Partizan, and they told us they had gone through all sorts of things: beatings, rape, robbery, all sorts of torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened in Cajnice? Why were you not exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two bits of news. They tried it on two occasions because we were twice in Cajnice and they twice tried. Once they said that allegedly ours, in inverted commas, that is, Bosniaks do not want us, that they want flour and sugar rather than us. And the second piece of news, and we were told that by the one who headed that exchange, and they called him Serdar. He had a cockade, a big fur cap, a long beard, and I think he was under the influence of drugs, but I'm not sure. And he said, "Well, those others have nobody to exchange for because they're all out because ours had killed them all." And he said that nobody should hurt us, because we were afraid that they might kill us, too, and we were waiting there to see what would happen. We hoped that they might let us go through Pljevlja, through the good offices of some authorities in Cajnice, but they failed to do that. And about that time, a BBC team arrived and they took down our names, and then I remember they really helped us a great deal in this way. But they took us back to Foca because the thing failed, and we were all taken back to Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All groups, the detainees from KP Dom and the women and elderly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you returned to the KP Dom, who received you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were received by Gagovic, I can't remember now whether his first name was Radislav or Rade. Something like that at any rate. Gagovic entered the bus and said to us that we had to go back, that we had to get all our things out again, all the stuff we had taken from Cajnice - we had also received something in Cajnice - and that we'd have to wait for the next exchange. Rade Gagovic received us. He's the person I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what position did he have in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, Mitar Rasovic, who was commander of the guards, and Gagovic entered our room, Room 15, and Mitar introduced Gagovic as the deputy warden of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet this Mr. Gagovic again that you could see what his position was with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him a few times. I saw him wearing civilian clothes then when he entered our room, but I also saw him sometimes wearing things like commando clothes, something like that, but I didn't have much contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are just checking the list. Maybe my colleagues can find out the person on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean -- the name has already been given.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to give you the number, and it's the number 79 on P3. You see Rade Gagovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how old Mr. Gagovic was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A young-ish man, say 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We do not need to go into details of labour done in the KP Dom. My question would only be: Did you yourself have to work in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had to if I was told to. I remember at first I went to Brod Na Drini to unload flour. I tried to lift a sack of flour. I couldn't. I fell. I almost fainted altogether. A friend was there, a former friend of mine, who was in charge, was there, a former friend of mine, a Serb. He let me go. They returned me. I didn't have to unload these sacks. Then they let me do something else: clean up in the kitchen. I couldn't even do that anymore. Later on, when I recovered a bit, I cleaned the compound. At some points I myself asked to work, because those who went out to work would get an additional slice of bread. That's why many of us asked to work, so that we would get this extra slice of bread. That's why I had also asked to work - to sweep, to carry baskets, whatever I could do - and that is how I sometimes got an extra slice of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know a person Murat Islambasic, and could you tell us what work he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that person. He was a driver. They would take him out on his own and return him again on his own. He drove a truck for the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know -- did you ever speak to him? Was he, for instance, in your room, and did he tell you where he drove the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were together in room 21. We slept on two adjacent beds. He didn't want to talk then. He didn't want to say where he went, what he did. At one moment, though, he started limping on purpose, because he wanted to get away from that job. He wanted to dodge it all together. He told me he was bluffing. He even started walking with a crutch, whatever. When we were both released, then he told me where he was taken and what he had to drive. He drove ammunition. He was on the first truck so that there would not be ambushes in terms of mines, whatever. He went to Kalinovik, Preljuca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden of the KP Dom during your time of detention. Who was the pre-war warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radojica Tesovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was the former warden replaced? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume since Mr. Tesovic, in all these pre-election activities, remained on the list of the SDP - that is to say, he did not go for the SDS - and I don't think he could hold any position.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you please come closer to the microphone again. The interpreters are having difficulty hearing you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tesovic, did he continue to work in the KP Dom during your confinement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him at the KP Dom. I think he was in charge of one unit, the furniture factory. It was then called Drina. He was in charge of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned Mr. Gagovic. What function did Mr. Todovic have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know officially what his position was, but he was like our boss, to all the detainees and to all the guards, it seemed to me. He was in contact with us and with the guards. He assigned people to do things. He told everyone what they had to do and he could also send people to solitary confinement straight away. He would see them in the compound and send them straight off to an isolation cell. A few of my colleagues were sent off that way. It seems to me that he had some kind of executive powers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him in the KP Dom, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember what he had the first time, but he wore civilian clothes. He wore an SMB uniform, he wore camouflage uniforms, he wore blue uniforms, but civilian clothes mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was Mitar Rasevic, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw him in the KP Dom, what did he wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A uniform, a blue police uniform, the kind that was worn by the police beforehand. I know that before, Mitar was also commander of the police guards in the prison. When I say "beforehand," I'm referring to the pre-war period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards, were they also the former prison guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones I knew personally and the ones I saw down there, I know for myself about them, but judging -- according to what I heard later, everybody seemed to have been a prison guard before as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the prison guards wear? What kind of clothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore blue. Later on it became fashionable to wear camouflage, but they mostly wore blue uniforms. And there were those, though, who wore these camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These camouflage uniforms that you saw on the guards, were they the blue camouflage of the police or were they camouflage of the military forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the military forces. They were green.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those persons you just mentioned - Todovic, Rasevic and the guards - how did they treat the detainees? How did they behave towards you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said about Todovic, so there's no need to repeat that. Not only towards me, but towards everyone. I'll give an example. Once there was a man from my room. His name was Sandal. He was also ill. I really can't remember his first name now. He asked Savo directly. Savo was passing by the stairs and I was there. I was cleaning. And he said, "Neighbour, can you help me? Can't you see I'm dying?" He was an elderly man. They were neighbours. They were from the same village, allegedly. That's what he told me later. He only looked at him and said, "Back to the room." He made him go back to the room. This man, Sandal, died soon after that at the KP Dom. That can be said about Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this incident occur? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime around the beginning of 1993, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have not yet mentioned: How did the guards treat the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From one case to another, it varied. There were different Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. guards. Some were bad, others were less bad. I've had experience with the ones who were bad and the ones who were less bad. Some were not very forthcoming. They didn't even want to listen. They didn't even want to receive any requests that we would give in order to be taken further. Some forced people to go to an isolation cell. Well, not me. But if they would catch them getting into the line again to get an extra slice of bread, they would be sent to an isolation cell invariably. Obrenovic, this man, was sent to an isolation cell by a guard once. Once when we were getting out of the dining room, this one detainee took a walnut. It was a young walnut. And this Obrenovic sent him to an isolation cell because of that walnut. That's what I can say about Obrenovic. Then there was this Zoran Matovic. From the very outset, he carried around something like a baseball bat. The other prisoners said that he used it for beating too. I heard about Burilo too. He did not beat me, but that he beat just about everybody else. There were those who mistreated people psychologically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he would come and say, "You balija," and other things. I wouldn't mention that. You know, referring to their mothers and sisters, next of kin. "You won't get out of here. You don't belong here." I mean, they were referring to Foca. And then they were saying that they wouldn't get out of the KP Dom. Jovo Savic figured prominently in this respect. There were also those who would help, but they were exceptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when was Mr. Krnojelac the warden of the KP Dom? When was he replaced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he was replaced, did the conditions in the KP Dom change? Did the behaviour of the guards and Mr. Todovic change?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the International Red Cross also came on several occasions, so we got toothpaste, toothbrushes for them, means for hygiene, sometimes even cigarettes, underwear so that we could change. And that's around the time when there was this change of wardens too. Then we had medical care, regular medical care. The food got much better. I mean, much better; it was a bit heavier, greasier, so to speak. There was more bread. We could take baths once or twice in a month. Once. Then our bed linen was changed. They washed our bed linen. So the difference was drastic until mid-1993 and after mid-1993. I personally experienced something. I was sent for medical examinations to the local hospital, and I was actually taken there and these medical examinations were carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that after Mr. Krnojelac was replaced that you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I know that warden Sekulovic helped me go there, the one who was Mr. Krnojelac's successor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the behaviour of the guards and Mr. Todovic, did it change after Mr. Sekulovic arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They locked us up less in rooms then. We even could go for a walk. We weren't locked up in the rooms all the time. The behaviour of the guards changed, and how. Todovic was far more reserved. He didn't show up very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the guards, you said the behaviour changed. In which way? What became different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started talking to us. They were forthcoming. Even if we did something that was irregular, they let it be. You could even trade with them then, with the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were detained until August 1994. How could you leave the KP Dom? How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me to get ready and to come to the gate. A guard came to fetch me. I came to the gate. And then I saw warden Sekulovic. He saw me off. He said, "I wish you the best of luck. If it succeeds, it will succeed." That's how he put it. Before that -- I mean it was during those days that I was supposed to undergo surgery at our hospital. I'm going to tell you one more thing. A man in my room, Sefko Kubat, died from the same illness. He was operated on, but I agreed to this surgery nevertheless. I already mentioned this. Sekulovic, through a prisoner, FWS-73, who went to his apartment to repair something for him, said that the warden felt sorry for me. Sekulovic knew me. I didn't know him, to tell you the truth. And he said that he felt sorry for me. He said that he saw that I was dying, because I simply couldn't recover from the very outset. And then he said, "We'll try to do something with him," and that's how I was sent for this exchange, probably thanks to warden Sekulovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions that the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to wish the witness a good morning and to introduce myself. I'm Miroslav Vasic, attorney at law, one of the Defence counsel for the accused Milorad Krnojelac. My first question would relate to the statements that you gave to the investigator of the OTP. Did you give your first statement to the investigator of the OTP on the 17th of August, the 18th of August, the 5th of September, 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give two statements to the investigator of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. On two or three occasions. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After making these statements, did you read them and sign them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo when I finished, I read something. I glanced at it, but I didn't read it in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign every page of these statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 23rd of August, 1994, did you give a statement at the Security Centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read and sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you talk to a journalist, whose name I'll give you presently, that is, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he publish this interview (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to read part of your statement to the investigator of the OTP, and you will tell me whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just before you do that, did that interview identify this witness by name?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the interview with the investigator of the OTP? Oh, the newspapers you mean, the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have an excerpt from this newspaper that the Prosecutor gave me. His name is not mentioned, but it is possible that he was identified in the text. I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I think we'd better redact the reference to the paper. It would be the clearest identification of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Vasic, but it seemed to me a rather vital issue on protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In order to facilitate matters for the interpreters, this is the part of the statement from the 30th of May. On page 4, it is the last paragraph, and on page 5, the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you state the following to the investigators of the OTP: "I knew that Savo Todovic was the real boss in the KP Dom. I knew him before the war only by sight and knew he was employed at the KP Dom as some kind of clerk. During the time I was detained there, he was in charge of the prisoners. He decided who was to be taken to which room. I don't know what his official title or position was, but everybody called him the boss. Even the guards addressed him so. As far as I can remember, he was present at the KP Dom all the time, even at night. "Todovic had dark hair and was balding. At first he had a short beard and later on a long one. He was of medium height and very well built. He sometimes wore civilian clothes and sometimes an SMB uniform. Later, he wore a camouflage uniform. "Savo Todovic once ordered me to go to a solitary confinement cell. I was there for 15 days because I had exchanged goods with the other prisoners. This was only an excuse because everybody did that. While there, Todovic asked me to give a statement admitting to something, which I would not do. He told me I would die in the cell." Is that what you stated to the investigator of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of it is correct except for one word, that "I" came to the conclusion that he was the real boss. I mean, I could not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you say that he was the real boss?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is how we saw him. We were afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in the English text, we also have the words "real boss." So did you say that, that you really were afraid -- it doesn't say you were really afraid of him and that is how you perceived him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot know what Savo Todovic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. I think the time has come to say this to the witness. You must remember, sir, that you, both you and Mr. Vasic are speaking the same language. The interpreters have to translate the question and the answer, so would you please pause before the answer to enable them to catch up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to a part of your statement which deals with events in 1991. Did you tell the Tribunal, its investigators, that as of 1991, both Serbs and Muslims began to arm themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also say to the Tribunal's investigator that the Serbs were doing it through the SDS, and Muslims through the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, is -- are you familiar with the name of Mr. Sahinpasic, called Saja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that when the war ended, he said for the press and for television that he was the one who had armed the Muslim people in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard those stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you said that on the 7th of April, exchange of fire began. You said that Serb forces were firing from one side on Sukovac and Siste. Did you tell the Tribunal's investigator that from Sukovac and Siste, the Muslims returned the fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember because I could not, I could not see. What I saw was really shells flying in that direction, but I also learnt that the other side returned the fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also say that it was a bus driver who told you that the Muslim artillery was on one side and the Serb artillery on the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I was coming back from Sarajevo, yes, there was this driver who said that it was already public. And he said that the Serb positions are in Zabrana, and that the Muslim positions are at Siste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the gentleman that you are mentioning now, this Bajo, what ethnicity is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I guess he's a Serb or possibly a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who were the most prominent figures in the SDA and SDS in Foca prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can, yes, because I knew a number of them personally. Do you want names? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, Miro Stanic. I knew him personally, and I met him on various occasions. He was then the president of the SDS. I knew Mr. Radojica Mladenovic. Mr. Petko Cancar, I knew him, too, and I knew many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps give us a name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Taib Lojo. He died. He was the president of the SDA. I knew Sahinpasic and a number of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from this list, can you help me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there should be a name for me to say something because I cannot give out the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is he under a number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you meaning the exhibit -- I'm sorry, the annexure C to the indictment? I've forgotten the exhibit number. Is that the list you want him to consult?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The list of protected witnesses which were shown to the witness with the numbers for witnesses, that is it. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The witness himself has pointed out he can't use their names, but you're satisfied if he goes to that list and refers to the numbers? There are only three on his list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness said they were not the persons under those numbers, and it's none of those on that list. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain? One witness has already testified here in The Hague, and I'd like to mention him. Should I?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, then I would like to suggest that the witness writes down the name of that witness so that then we can identify him by the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would be a good idea. We need some more paper for the witness, please. We'd better see whether we have got an FWS number for that; if not, we'll give him a new pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, FWS-111, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there a consolidated list of all these FWS numbers that we could perhaps have access to, not right now, but at some stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have the list in the trial binder. It should be in the first trial binder, there's a complete list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I remember that at the previous trial; I hadn't seen it here. I'll look for it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement here, you said what the SDS thought and pursued regarding the homogenisation of people. Did the SDA pursue the same kind of policy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us which were the objectives of the SDS. And what were the SDA objectives at that time, on the eve of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I followed -- as I covered an election rally of the SDA, I mean officially I did it, officially covered it, at the -- I learned from the requests of the listeners that they were asking for "their Bosnia" or something, I don't know. But the then president of the SDA, Mr. Izetbegovic, said that that was not possible, that it was not possible, that they wanted a joined democratic state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember if after what you have just told us that Mr. Izetbegovic had said, that he added the words -- the word "unfortunately"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. "Unfortunately not right now. Unfortunately, but that is not possible, that what is possible is only a democratic and joined state of Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you heard on the radio how the JNA members and paramilitaries were entering Visegrad, Zvornik, or had entered Visegrad and Zvornik. Was that before Mr. Murat Sabanovic wanted to blow up the dam in Visegrad or after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't remember, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because this was in the media too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I listened. I heard about that, but I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the eve of the armed conflicts a division, a rift took place between the Muslims and Serbs in Foca and they even began to patronise different coffee pubs. Could you tell us which were the coffee bars which were frequented by Muslims, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I only patronised about four coffee bars. Perhaps I would drop by some others, but rarely. And for instance, I can tell you where I went. Amadeus was a multi-ethnic coffee pub. Its owner was a democratic. D-Mol was also a reformist place, because it was jointly owned by Serbs and Muslims, and so people there were mixed again. And as for others, I really did not patronise them often. I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of a restaurant run by Mr. Grujicic? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there often. It was called Dzam [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would you call it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb, a Serb restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me. It was at that time when the split took place, and could you tell us where did the Muslims go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they went to a place called Nocturno, which is somewhere in Gornje Polje, Nocturno. I've just remembered another Serb place. It was called La Linea, and that was where only -- or Linea. It was patronised only by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to go back to the time when you left Foca temporarily and went to Zubovici. You said that you had a weapon. Did you take it along when you went to Zubovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have it when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us here that when you arrived in KP Dom you were interviewed by investigator Koprivica the very next day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the very next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been perhaps a week later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else attend that interrogation except Mr. Koprivica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the three of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that in your statement to the public security centre in Sarajevo you said that on that occasion there was also present somebody called Petko Gasevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Petko Gasevic, but he had only brought a drink for my father and left immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him only by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear a uniform on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a military man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really tell you anything about Petko Gasevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Here you testified that the investigator Koprivica did not ask you anything, that he merely signed a guarantee saying that he vouched for you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor and the Security Centre in Sarajevo, you said that you were asked if you were a member of a political party, if you had a weapon, your whereabouts during the conflict. Were you asked that by that Koprivica? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a general question, but Koprivica knew that I was not a member of the party, he knew that I was not armed, that I had never fired a single shot, so he never asked me those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you said then to the Prosecutor's investigator, was that account by general statement? Because it says here that you stated that you were interrogated and your father not, in general.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my father had arrived before me. I said so. And he interrogated my father. And when my father answered, he said, "I know everything, and you don't have to answer any questions," so that he did not ask me any questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did your father then tell you that he asked him questions about all this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the answer because the witness overlapped with the Prosecutor -- with the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, we've lost the answer there because your question came in on top of it. Did you hear the answer yourself? The question was: Did your father then tell you that he asked him questions about all this? Did you hear what the answer was?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is: We did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Take care, please. Do not weigh in with your next question until the interpreters have caught up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the public security station, did you say that Muslims were interrogated also by the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It escapes me now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you say something along those lines to the journalist Midhat Plivcic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I'd like to read out to you only one sentence from this text in the media: "Until August 1992, the detained prisoners were also interrogated by members of the Foca military police." Evidently, after they broke into the SDA offices, they found there the list of all the SDA members in Foca and all the activists.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how in the same article you said that you were interrogated by the former police inspectors in Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said here, when my learned friend asked you whether you had been interrogated by military or police investigators, you answered that it was the policemen who interrogated you. How did you come to that conclusion, that they did not come from the army but from the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I knew Koprivica, because I knew Vladicic, I knew Starovic too. I didn't know what his position was. And they all worked for the Foca police before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that one of them worked for the SDK, for the public auditing office, not for the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I knew about two of them, so it could have been Starovic who worked perhaps for the SDK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But here in this article you used the word "former policemen." Does this mean that they had been transferred to some other formations, according to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I do not know what office they held at that time. I knew that they were policemen before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But does that mean that one could conclude they were military police investigators and the -- because you say that you could not draw any conclusion from their clothes, you did not know what their new status was, so perhaps there is this possibility as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not much of a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is possible, even if not very likely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know where this is heading, Mr. Vasic. It doesn't seem to be helping us very much. The question is not whether it's possible. Anything is possible. If there's something relating to an issue which has to be proved, the question is whether it is proved beyond Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reasonable doubt, which raises an issue of a reasonable possibility being to the contrary. But I don't really think that you're going to get anywhere by arguing this with the witness. That seems to be an appropriate time. We'll take a break now. We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me? Can I begin now? Thank you. In your statement in response to my learned colleague's question, you said that you were interviewed once while you were staying at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you said to the investigators of the OTP in your statement dated the 30th of May, 1999, the following: "I was interrogated many times during my detention. The interrogations took place on the second floor of the administrative buildings. During these interrogations, they did not beat me." Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "once," I was referring to the investigators, Koprivica specifically. On one occasion in connection with a problem that occurred, when I was keeping this radio set that we listened to the news on, Savo Todovic and Miro Prodanovic interrogated me in connection with that. Miro Todovic -- Miro Prodanovic and Savo Todovic did not beat me ever, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here you said "many times." You gave this statement to the best of your recollection and to the best of your ability. That's what it says there. Has your memory become refreshed now, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not say that for sure because it is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it perhaps jog your memory if I were to show this to you, to show you this statement, what it says there? This is your signed statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need, as I said. So it was twice, once by Mr. Koprivica officially, and this other one was probably official, too, this second occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what it says here in this statement is not true. It says that that is what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is not correct, then, because that is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same statement, it says that this first interrogation that you were taken out for took place on the 18th of April, 1992, "On the second day of my stay at the KP Dom." Today you said that you were first taken out for an interrogation after seven days. Which one of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been, because during those days I was in Room 12 and we could not get out. That is to say, a week later. Perhaps it was not translated right, but that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state to the investigator of the OTP that you saw Milorad Krnojelac three times altogether?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement here, you said that that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. I do apologise, Your Honour. In the transcript, it does not say that he saw Mr. Krnojelac during daytime. It doesn't say so in the transcript, that is 34:13, but the witness did say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd better take it up with the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you saw Milorad Krnojelac for a total of three times while you were at the KP Dom, and all three times during daytime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the last time you saw Mr. Krnojelac, you saw him in uniform with a belt and weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And an officer's bag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see, and an officer's bag too. Why did you not say this to anyone before? And you gave two statements to the OTP and one to the security station, and you gave all of them to the best of your recollection and to the best of your ability. That's what it says in all these statements.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably didn't ask me about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned colleague here did not ask you, either, whether Mr. Krnojelac wore a belt and weapons and a military bag, and you nevertheless said so. Did something jog your memory in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your memory better in 1994 when you gave your statement in the public security station and in 1997 when you did so to the investigator of the OTP, or is your memory better today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked specifically here about Mr. Krnojelac, so I remembered a bit more, whereas over there, nobody asked me about Mr. Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about Mr. Krnojelac there too. You only mentioned one meeting, but you mentioned three here. Seeing him three times, I mean. My colleague here did not ask you about weapons or the bag, either. Do you have any explanation for all of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked here whether he wore a uniform or civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the investigator of the OTP, you mentioned that Mr. Krnojelac wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With what I already said, pistol, a small bag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not state that to the investigator of the OTP. Bearing in mind that you gave these statements to the best of your recollection, that means that at that time you did not remember that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, my memory need not have been the best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I mean, I wasn't asked about it. Had I said so, I probably would have said so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about 1999 in your second statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you mentioned here that you wrote requests for the warden to receive you. You did not mention that fact in any one of your statements, either your statement given to the public security station or the two statements you gave to the investigator of the OTP. Is the reason the same, or is it simply that you remember just now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it now. I mean, not this very minute, but when I was informed that I would testify, that I would be a witness, I went through things in my mind, that's a fact, and I mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you run things through your mind also before you gave statements to the investigators of the OTP, to the police in Sarajevo, because after all, we are talking about the period between 1994 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered the questions they put to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you mention to someone what you mentioned here, that you tried to call Mr. Krnojelac? I mean, did you ever mention this before yesterday? And that's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Krnojelac was arrested, I remembered a few things. I remembered where I used to see him and how I used to see him. Then I talked to people a bit about Mr. Krnojelac. I talked to the members of my family, my friends, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac was arrested in 1998 and you gave your second statement to the investigator of the OTP in 1999, that is to say, after these consultations. In that statement, nevertheless, you did not mention what you said today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, these were not consultations. This was just chatting. So I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your father was released in May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's question, you said that you thought that your opinion was because the Red Cross had registered them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you also mentioned that you knew that this documentation that was compiled by the Red Cross was taken away by some members of the military or the paramilitary, the Serb forces - I don't know - and that the Red Cross no longer had these documents or the vehicle that they had driven in before that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you agree with me if I say that, bearing this in mind, it is not very logical that they were released because of the Red Cross lists, because these lists were not in the hands of the organisation that had compiled them but in the hands of the Serb forces. Can you agree with me, then, that that conclusion that that is the reason is not logical?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not like to draw any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but in response to my learned colleague's question, you drew a conclusion here that that was the reason, that that is why the list was compiled.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can draw a conclusion. If they registered one room and they started registering others, and then if they broke off abruptly, they probably had a reason why they had to break off and why this was taken away from them. I assume that they took them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said yesterday is only what you concluded, what you inferred, and whether it's logical or not is another question, but it is only what you inferred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me: After you came to the KP Dom, were there any ethnic Serbs there as well who were serving their sentences, those pronounced in the former Yugoslavia, in the courts in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated yesterday that through some guards you tried to get in touch with the warden again. Can you give us the names of these guards through whom you made such attempts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through several of them, but I really cannot remember now who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me at least one name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention four or five names: Pljevaljcic, Obrenovic, Milic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you gave them these requests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't remember now. I don't know which ones of them exactly, but I did give these requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give any to Risto Ivanovic, a guard, also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember now. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that these guards that you mentioned are the ones that you remember, but you cannot remember having given them these requests precisely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your answer mean that the names are the names of the guards whom you remember, but you are not sure whether they were the ones to whom you gave the requests for the warden to receive you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it could have been one of them, some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they knew me a bit better, it was easier for me to address them. That is why I mentioned their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that when you came to the KP Dom that there were quite a few soldiers there with different uniforms from areas that are outside the municipality of Foca. Can you tell me when these soldiers left the KP Dom? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the beginning of May. Perhaps they stayed for another 10 or 15 days, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you mentioned that you did not have adequate medical care. Did you say to the investigators of the OTP the following: "Since I had some stomach problems before the war, during detention I had lost weight and I had to be treated in prison. We would give the guards a list of the detainees who were ill and then they took us to the clinic, where the doctor examined the ill and prescribed medicines. Very often there weren't any medicines. However, I was fortunate to have known the doctors and the pharmacists, so I was treated on time."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to show you your statement dated the 17th and 18th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. August and the 5th of September and the 16th of November that you gave to the investigators of the OTP and that you signed on every page, to the best of your knowledge, would you remember that you had stated that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, we are just talking about time. Until the end of 1992, that was not the case. However, when Sekulovic came later, that's the way it was, and that's what I already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you stated here that you were treated on time, that is to say that your problems started then. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only referring to the time period that I mentioned here, because that is when I got medical treatment. In 1992, when it was most difficult, I did not get any medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand the terms correctly, to treat "on time," that has to do with the beginning of the problems that you had at the KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is maybe what it says there, but that's not the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you said to the investigators of the OTP is not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way it was. Maybe it's a question of the translation. Perhaps they did not refer rightly to the time pertaining to my treatment. Let me add something else. In 1992, I did not know any doctor, so I cannot say that I knew anyone. I did know the pharmacist, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am now going to read to you what you stated to the public security station in terms of your treatment: "I got ill, and after being examined by a doctor, I was told that I had to go to hospital. Dr. Cedo Dragovic examined me. However, allegedly there was no room in hospital, so I was prescribed infusion. I was prescribed eight infusions within four days." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. That is not correct in terms of the number of drips I got. I got only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher help me, please. Could he please give the witness this statement so that he could say whether the signature on the bottom of the page is his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That, of course, is the English version, is it not? That was the one that would have been signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. This is the B/C/S version that I got from the OTP, ID 307, whereas the English version is ID 307A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've been through this, I think, many times before, but do you realise that what happens is the witness or the proposed witness gives his statement in B/C/S, it's translated into English and recorded in English? He signs the English version, which is then retranslated back into B/C/S. Now, if we're dealing with minor details in that with two different stages of translation, the weight to be afforded to any minor discrepancy is very small. So if it's an important matter, you proceed; but if it's not, may I suggest you move on to your next point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
