utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is actually not the case in this -- in relation to this statement. This is a B/C/S statement given to the Bosnian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the original is in B/C/S, and the witness signed the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're luckier than we are because I don't think it's been made clear in the cross-examination. You proceed, Mr. Vasic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I was about to say the same thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature, yes, right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your signature at the end of this page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give us the name of the pharmacist who issued the medicines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Jokanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony here, you said that during your stay in KP Dom, you changed rooms. Could you give us the rooms that you were in and at what times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the times, but I'll give you the numbers of rooms. In 12 to begin with, 11, in 15, 21, 16. I don't know. I changed them often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you tell us, for instance, the years, in 1992, 1993, 1994, which rooms were you in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I told you, I started Room 12, in Room 12, I moved on to my father's in 11. Then I went to 15 until September 1992, so August, September 1992. And then, unfortunately, a number of people were taken for exchange, that is, only seven or eight were left, and then we were moved to another room, and then I went to 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I was in 16. It is working room. Room 20. I was in the working room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today that on one occasion you heard a shot after a prisoner had been taken away. Did you also hear some shots on other occasions which had nothing to do with the taking away of the prisoners? Was there any gunfire opened in KP Dom that had nothing to do with people being taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Mr. Zulfo Veiz was in the same room with you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take him from your room on that occasion when he did not come back from the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he taken to a ground-floor room where you had your meeting with Krnojelac, as you told us, on that occasion when he did not come back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard -- I guess that it is from that room that the beatings reached us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what room were you in when you heard shots related to the beatings that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Room 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you spoke about the exchange in Cajnice. You said that RJ and FWS-86 thought they had been sent there by Mr. Krnojelac. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever mention this fact before, before anyone; the OTP investigator or the Sarajevo police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In no statement of yours can one find this particular fact. We cannot find that either in the statement of the OTP or the police in Sarajevo. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an oversight. I must have said about it to the OTP investigators. As for the -- as for Sarajevo, their security service, I don't know, but I did mention it. I distinctly know that I mentioned the exchange in Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim that you said that, and the investigators forgot to write it down, that is, that they omitted to write it down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I'd put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today when asked by my learned friend about Mr. Tesovic, you said that, in your opinion, he did not insist on continuing as the warden of the KP Dom because he was a member of the reformist forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: SDP, not the reformist forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. Are you aware that immediately after the outbreak of the conflict, Mr. Tesovic took a group of Muslim prisoners to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is -- took a long time to make the trip?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that Mr. Tesovic, in August 1993, was appointed the head of the commercial unit of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know when, but I know that he was this manager because I saw him pass me by in the compound, within the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you said he was a member of the SDP, can you then explain it to us? How did this appointment come about, in your view, since the SDS still held the power at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to ask Mr. Tesovic about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant did you make some inferences about that? Did you think that he became manager after he stopped being an SDP member, or what did you -- what were your conjectures or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that you have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, why did he stop -- when you were asked why did Mr. Tesovic stop being the prison warden, you said he was a member of the SDP. Now my question is, is that your inference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my inference, but I can add also other names. Mr. Trado Konkadin [phoen] was manager of Maglic, and he had to stop being its manager because he was also on the SDP list. And there are other instances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm merely trying to show that my question was in line with your inference. If the SDS was still in power, and it was, then how could Mr. Tesovic be appointed the head of the commercial unit if the reason for his being dismissed from the position of the warden was his membership in the SDP? That is what I tried to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you. You know, I should say very well, that a wolf may change his skin but never his nature, and that that is the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about poor diet in the KP Dom. Did all of the prisoners, I mean of Muslim ethnicity, lose weight significantly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the early months of our stay there, yes, we all lost weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend asked you about list C, which you were shown. I should like to ask you about one name from that list, Mr. Munib Veiz. Did you see him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what room he was in when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him line up for the canteen, so I saw him outside, but I think that he was staying in room 13 or 11. But I only saw him during the line-up, and that was on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt later that he was missing, that he was gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when he went missing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really give you the exact date, but it was 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the name of Sefko Kubat today and you said that, unfortunately, he died. Could you tell us, when did he die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise; just one question more. It has to do with Mr. Kubat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he died of, what was the cause of his death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He suffered from stomach complaints. He was hospitalised, underwent surgery, then lived for a couple of months after that and then died.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I want to clarify two matters. Re-examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were, just a few minutes ago, you were at this part in relation to your examination conducted by Dr. Cedo Dragovic, as it is in the statement you gave to the Bosnian police. Do you remember any Dr. Cedo Dragovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember Dr. Cedo Dragovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember, did he examine you? And if so, when? Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was July. I think that the doctor came in July, and that was the first time I went to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he prescribe drips, as it is stated here, and did you receive treatment afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once. I was given only one infusion, not after that. And then Gojko Jokanovic gave me some tablets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other matter I would like to clarify is: You mentioned when you were asked that you had a weapon on you when you went to your sister's place in Zubovici. What kind of a weapon was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a pistol, Baretta; Baretta pistol which belonged to my wife's father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you take this weapon with you when you went to this house in Zubovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think I felt safer with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said also that when you were arrested you didn't have this pistol. Where was it? Did you give it back or where did it stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-182 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left it in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That is what we had to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may leave. If you'll just wait a moment before the blinds are pulled down so that you may leave the courtroom without being identified by the public. Is the next witness 82?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And are there protective measures for that witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No. That witness has not asked for any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Except a pseudonym, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: He did not request that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir, and we can have all the blinds up and the screen moved. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Examined by Ms. Kuo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm Rasim Taranin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: On the 17th of March, 1942 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you married, sir?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: A son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity are you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see on the transcript that the birth date was written down as 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the birth -- the year you were born again so we can get that corrected? What year were you born?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: 17th of March, 1942.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, on Monday, when you came here to the Tribunal, was there a short period of time when you came to the public gallery?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Here, you mean? I tried to, yes, to come and see a little, cast a look, but I was told to go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a portion of the trial?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, from a corner, but I couldn't really see very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Not very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I'd like to turn your attention to April of 1992. At that time, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I lived at the railway station called Zigovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from the centre of Foca was that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: About four kilometres, maybe five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who lived there with you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I lived there, and there were neighbours. I can give you their names, if need be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I meant who of your immediate family was there with you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: My brother and I shared the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your wife and son also live with you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I worked for a public enterprise called Izvor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I was the head of the machine department, that is, for the last ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, sir, when did the war in Foca start?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Better said, sometime on the 6th of April fire began to be exchanged on villages, and then on the 6th or 7th, I'm not quite sure, around 9.00 in the evening, shelling began or, rather, rockets were aimed at Focatrans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: At the time, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from Focatrans was that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Some 150, 200 metres from my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything when you saw the rockets falling on Focatrans?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: My family and I and my brother-in-law and his family, we fled to cellars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the cellars?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Until the morning. The rockets, the shelling, stopped sometime around 5.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: When the fire stopped, we and my family decided to go to my father-in-law because he was supposed to come in the evening and had failed to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did your father-in-law live?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: In the centre on Titovo Street, rather, right next to the SUP office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived -- was this an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived there, did anyone greet you, or did you meet anyone?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: There was his neighbour, Milovan Zivanovic, a retired teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity is he?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Orthodox, or better said, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: He said, "Where is your father-in-law? Isn't he with you?" And I said he wasn't and that was why we had come, to see if he was in his own home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zivanovic tell you what you should do?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: He told me to go upstairs to my father-in-law's flat, and if I had any weapons with me, to give them to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I had a hunting rifle, 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give it to him?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I gave him this rifle which was all cleaned and all, and I told him also, "Here are bullets, and you can see that the rifle is clean, so mind that you don't say that I fired from it or anything." And he said, "No problem. I know, I know you. I know you're a nice man," and he took over the weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you give your weapon to Mr. Zivanovic when he asked you? Was there any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: He said to me that we had to do this, that there are all kinds of members of the military, and somebody could say that you wanted to shoot or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at your father-in-law's place?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, all the time, until they came to pick me up, and then later this man came and took me to the KP Dom. That is to say, until the 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 27th of when?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that time, did you see soldiers in the area?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I was in the cellar all the time, one could say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the cellar of your father-in-law's house -- apartment building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was that cellar?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It was long, about as long as the building itself, 100 or 200 metres, except it was partitioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was hiding in the cellar with you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: In that part that we were in, there were three or four other families as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they Serb families or Muslim families?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: All were Muslim, all were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any soldiers come to the cellar to speak with you or to take anyone away?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: They tried to get in, but thanks to Milovan Zivanovic, I mean, he didn't allow them to get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any soldiers come and tell you not to be afraid?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a Nurko Nisic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I know him. He was with me in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, that morning I did not notice who took him, only later I was told that Nurko was taken away for questioning. I don't know who did it or how it was, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Nurko was in the cellar with you. Was he also there with his family?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, in relationship to the time that you were taken away, how soon before you were taken away Nurko Nisic was taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, before me. I'm not sure exactly when. He was in the cellar with me for about six days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were taken away on the 27th of April, 1992. Can you tell us how that happened?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: On the 27th of April, around 10.00, I went to take bread. I went to get bread from a bakery near the post office. There were lots of people there. The head of that shop, Nada, recognised me. I don't know what his last name was. He asked me to come in, and he gave me two fresh, hot loaves of bread, although I was not the one whose turn it was. We jumped the queue. And then he said, "You can pay later, never mind." Then by the borovo shop, I realised that there were three people behind me, following me. They called out my last name, "Taranin, stop." I pretended not to be able to hear them. He repeated, "Taranin, stop. Can you hear me?" I heard him. I stopped; I turned around. Mr. Kovac came, I think his name is Radomir, and he said, "Where have you been?" And I said, "I went to buy bread." And, "Where are you going now?" I said, "I'm going to my father-in-law's. That's where my family is." And he said, "Leave that bread, and you're coming with me to the KP Dom to make a statement." And that's exactly what I did. When I came I said to Milovan Zivanovic that they came to pick me up and that they were waiting for me outside. I was hoping that he would help me. I went to the apartment, and I left the bread. I told my family about this. They started crying. I went back downstairs, and I saw Milovan talking to these men. I heard Milovan say, "Don't take him. They know about him. Rasim is a good man. The command knows about him, too." And he said, "I'm not asking you about that. He's going to the KP Dom." He called the duty policeman, the policeman who was on duty then. I don't know exactly his name and surname, but I know his nickname. For ten or 15 years he was a professional policeman. His nickname is Coce. He ignited [as translated] the car. They put me in the back. This Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Radomir Kovac and another one, I don't know his name exactly, they took me to the KP Dom where the officer on duty was Koroman Slavko, who was a senior officer, and then there was also Ivanovic Risto by the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You mentioned that three men stopped you. One of them was Radomir Kovac. What were they wearing, do you remember? Were they wearing military clothes or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Military, military. It was a uniform. Military, all three of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they identify themselves by what authority they were taking you to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing. It was the way I told you about. They got me to the KP Dom without even touching me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please come close to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you bring your chair a little bit close to the microphones. The interpreters are having difficulty hearing you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the soldiers who took you to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, their very names show that they're Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, regarding the manner in which you were arrested, did you give a statement in 1995 to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I remember when I got out of the camp, sometime in October or November 1994 - I think it was October - that my own authorities, the MUP, asked me to give a statement, and I did. Then I came (redacted) I gave some kind of a statement. I don't know, to tell you the truth, what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came to the Tribunal on Monday to prepare for your testimony here, did you have a chance to review the statement that you gave in (redacted), for the first time, in your own language?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the statement, did it say that you were arrested in the cellar?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. That's what it says. I can't remember now. Maybe that is what it says, but that's not correct. It was the way I told you: I was buying bread, and as I was going towards my house, they called out my name. They caught me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reviewed your statement, did you find other things that you were surprised to read, things that you found to be inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, there were some things. I don't know. Maybe the translators made some mistakes, maybe I made some mistakes, maybe somebody misinterpreted what I said. There were some things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you were taken to KP Dom and you met there a Slavko Koroman and a Risto Ivanovic. Were they working at KP Dom? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I know them well, if I can put it that way. They are my great friends, both of them, and they did that job professionally. I don't know for how many years, but for a long time it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "that job," you meant that they worked at KP Dom before the war as well; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either of them say anything to you when you were brought to the KP Dom that day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, Slavko said to me, either ill-intentionally or maybe he was just joking, he said, "Where did you catch him?" They just left me there. And he said to me, "Turk, where did they catch you? Fuck all the gods you've got." And then somebody said, "Mr. Risto, Rasim is a good man. Take him to where his director is, room number 15."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was making all those comments, cursing you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: This thing that was said to me was said by Slavko Koroman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that surprise you that he said those things to you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, at first it did, but later he said, "I'm joking. Rasim is a good guy." Then I realised it was a joke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he said it was a joke, had the two men who had brought you already left?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: He took me by the hand and took me to number 15, upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where room 15 is located, what floor?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, when you enter the main gate, you go right upstairs, and on the left-hand side was room number 11. That's what it was called. And I went a bit to the right and then there was number 12. And then I took the stairs upstairs and that's where number 15 was. Opposite me was something like a health or whatever - what would I call it? - clinic for examinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In room 15, how many smaller rooms were there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Upstairs there were four rooms. Actually, there was one big room of about 30, 40 beds. Thirty, forty beds could fit in there. Then there was a small room where I would be staying. That was a small room with seven beds. And two rooms that were for taking a rest, smoking a cigarette. And then from that other room, there was a toilet that you could go to from there. So I think you could say that there were four rooms altogether, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in room 15? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly whether it was a month and a half or two. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Approximately about 13 or 14 months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the exact date when you were released from KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: You mean altogether or from Foca?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the date that you were taken away from KP Dom Foca.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but it was either the end of May or the month of June. I don't know the exact date when I went to Rudo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be 1993?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: We're talking about 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Shortly after your arrival at KP Dom, were you made to start working?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: After three or four days, they assigned me to carry flour from Ustikolina to Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's clarify that. How did you get to Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: A guard came in the morning and he said, "Taranin, get ready. You are going to work." He took me out of the room and at the gate I saw some 15 or so men. I thought we were going somewhere, but I didn't think of work really. He took me and three more men. They put us in a police van and they took us to Ustikolina. That is where we stood along an assembly line, and some of us were loading and others were unloading sacks of flour, and that's exactly what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Ustikolina, was it just you and the other three detainees in your car or did the whole group of 15 or 20 detainees also arrive at Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: At that time, there were four groups, because there were four trucks. I worked for four days. Well, now I cannot say whether there were four groups and four trucks every day. I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were loading and unloading sacks of flour, what were you loading onto?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Three consignments to Livade, a warehouse that belonged to the JNA, and it was a warehouse of flour and salt and things like that for Perucica. Those were three consignments. And the fourth one was on the fourth day at the headquarters of the Perucica company, where the Serif Lojo barracks used to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So am I to understand that when you were loading flour in Ustikolina, it was onto lorries to take them to Foca, to these warehouses?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you then driven to Foca to unload the sacks of flour once they were delivered to the warehouses you described?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: That's where we were, on trucks. And then you would put the tarpaulin over us and the sacks of flour, whereas the guard was with the driver in front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you did this for four days. Did you have any choice about working in this way?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I didn't even try anything. I didn't dare say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to clarify things, the warehouses that you described these flour sacks being delivered, was that also in Foca town?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: That does belong to the town of Foca. For example, the Livade warehouse is two kilometres away from the centre, whereas the Serif Lojo barracks is not even a kilometre away from the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the work; do you know?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly. We were taken by a guard, a policeman, from the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were working, were you being guarded by anyone?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who? What was that person or persons wearing?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: These were policemen from the KP Dom who worked before, too, and they had the same kind of uniform that they wore before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with a Savo Todovic during this time?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, on the fourth day, when I finished working in the afternoon, I returned to the camp. He was sitting outside on a chair where these people would usually sit. He said "Taranin, how are things going, this job?" I said, "Well --" and he said, "Is it better to be a boss or a worker?" I was thinking about what I should say. If I would put it the other way around, I was afraid I'd get in trouble, so I thought that I should say the truth. I said it was better to be the boss rather than a worker. And he said, "No more bossing around, there's only work left." And then I went on into the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Savo Todovic had an official function at the KP Dom during this time?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: He was deputy warden, the deputy of Warden Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that he was the deputy warden?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: That's what everybody told us, the guards and also when people talked amongst themselves. As soon as I got in, I was told that Krnojelac was warden and that Savo Todovic was deputy. Savo Todovic was in the KP Dom before that as well, but I don't know which post he held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Krnojelac before the war?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: As a citizen, as a math teacher at the school. I don't know whether he taught physics as well. However, I cooperated with his school and with the principal of his school, Darko; and also, our machinery took away the waste that had to be taken away from his school. I don't know whether I should tell you about all of this. Joko Gasic [phoen] was my boss, and we gave them a subsidised price so that there would be more money for the students so they could go on excursions during the summer and things like that. And every time I went to see them, they were real nice to me. They'd offer me coffee, and they were good to me, and I would like to thank them on this occasion as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- who were you told -- who told you that Krnojelac was the warden of KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: All the guards, all the guards in the compound and the policemen. I mean, whenever anything had to be done, they said that they had to ask Krnojelac. That's what they told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you surprised to see that Krnojelac was the warden of KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, at first, because I thought that he was a nice man, a teacher, a math teacher, an educator, and to take that kind of a difficult job after that, I was a bit surprised. But then, sometimes people take jobs. Maybe somebody imposed it on him. But I would never have done that, if anybody were to ask me something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see Krnojelac at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: About three or four times I saw him. Twice I took his breakfast to him because I worked at the kitchen then. Actually, I was not the one who found that food. It was Krsto Krnojelac who was sometimes leader of the shift. He would prepare the food. And he ate very little; he didn't eat much. Usually he would have two scrambled eggs, and two times while I was there, I took it to him. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to make sure that the record is clear. You mentioned that there was a Krnojelac who was a cook. What relation was the Krnojelac who was the cook to Krnojelac the warden? Were they related at all?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: They should be related. Krsto Krnojelac was a professional cook, at least for me at the time while I worked there. He was very fair to me. I think that they are closely related.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the first name of Krnojelac the warden?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: You know, to tell you the truth, I can't remember now. I don't know, maybe I'll remember later. I'll tell you then. I know exactly what his name is, but just give me some time. I'm not sure. I don't want to say this just off the cuff, just like that. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. You said that you brought him breakfast. Where did you bring the breakfast to him?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: A room where they ate separately, the guards and these people from the directorate and these policemen who had superior rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they ate separately from whom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: They ate separately in another room. They had a room of their own, and in this other room there were the detainees, the prisoners. That was a different room. That's not where they ate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they -- did you serve the same food to both the detainees and the prison staff?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the difference in food?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: First of all, there was a separate pot for us, the inmates - I don't know what to call us - and then there was another pot for the officers, the guards, these other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac, the warden, other than the times that he came to eat?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, while the year I was there, actually one year and two months or so, 13 or 14 months, I saw him about three or four times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him those three or four times, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, he'd come to have breakfast at that time, usually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that the record is clear, when you first said that you saw him only two times, did you mean that those were the two times you saw him at breakfast?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I was referring to the two times I served him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the three or four times, is that in addition to those two times?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No, no. All of this put together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Krnojelac other than when he came to eat?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time for us to go eat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. We'll resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the lunch break, we were talking about Krnojelac, the warden. I have a few more questions about him. When you saw him at the KP Dom, was he dressed in uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: When I saw him, then he was in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you move up against the desk again, please, sir, so that they can hear you more clearly through the microphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there also times when you saw him in civilian clothes inside the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I didn't see him often. As I said, he came four or five times, and on all those occasions he was in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Krnojelac, the warden, did you ever speak with him or did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No, although when I arrived in the KP Dom, I did ask to speak to him. I asked him to receive me to find out why I had been brought there, but I never made it to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke with investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995, you said that Krnojelac was the director only on paper. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I used the word "director," but he was a warden, because that is how we addressed him, and guards had also told us that they referred to him as the warden, and that is how we concluded that he was a warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the part of the statement where you say he was the warden only on paper -- first of all, did you say that he was the warden only on paper?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, from what was going on in the KP Dom, yes, it did seem that he was the warden on paper, because all the rest, with guards and all the other contacts, all the other jobs were performed there by Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke with the state security office in Sarajevo in 1994, did you tell them that Todovic was the one who was in command at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't remember if that was how I worded it then, but I do know that he practically ran things more in the KP Dom than Krnojelac, called Mico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the relationship was between Krnojelac, the warden, and Savo Todovic at KP Dom at that time?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I couldn't say really. All I know is that Todovic ran all those important things there. Whether Krnojelac had authorised him or had he authorised himself, that is something I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you described how you -- the first task that you were made to do. The first labour was loading and unloading sacks of flour. Were you asked to do something else after that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: After that, two or three days later, this work brigade, the construction brigade, had to go to pull down a school, and I sometimes joined that group. Sometimes we were seven or eight or twelve. And that is what we went to do, to pull down that school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer or were you simply taken to do that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: They came to take me, a guard, and said, "Taranin, you're going with a group to do that," and of course I had no right to say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the school located?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It was next to Serif Lojo's monument, or rather, next to the health centre in Aladza, near Aladza mosque in the park, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see the condition of the Aladza mosque at that time?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: When we began demolishing the school, removing the tiles and other things from the roof, around the 10th or 15th -- no, I'm not quite sure. But until the 15th, the Aladza still stood up, or at least the tower, or as we Muslims call it, the minaret. It was standing until sometime around the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: There was a break of two or three days, that is, we didn't go to that school. We were not given any reason for that. We thought that perhaps there was some drill or exercise in the town. But after two or three days, we went back to that school to continue pulling it down, and somebody -- I could not see it because I was piling some tiles, but somebody, during a short break, said that Aladza mosque was gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see that for yourself?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Later on, yes, the next day. One couldn't really watch much because the guards wouldn't let us, but later on as we climbed the roof, yes, we all cast looks in that direction, and we saw that, yes, the mosque was gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe exactly what you were doing in terms of the school? You mentioned taking tiles down. What were you doing to the school?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It was roof tiles that we are taking off, and then the various timber elements. We were all putting it -- bringing it down. We were simply demolishing the school, pulling down the school. For a while I was taking off roof tiles and then piling them up, and timber and other construction material. True, I was a worker there, but there was a tailor -- a carpenter there, and he was the leader of our brigade, or I don't know what you call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why you were taking the school down?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Not really. I heard various comments, and even some guards, they were saying that they were pulling down the school in order to build a church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the process of tearing down the school, were you using your bare hands, or did you have machines or tools?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, we had some picks which helped us to break something off, things like that. I mean, nothing much, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether that school was a mixed, ethnically-mixed school, or a predominantly Muslim or a predominantly Serb school before the war?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It was the first school; it was the oldest school there. Everybody was enrolled there. Everybody attended that school, and that includes me. All the ethnic groups, there were no divisions or anything. True, I mean, there were not too many different ethnic groups. There were Muslims and Serbs and a few Croats, but very few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days did you work on that school, or when did you stop?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I worked there for about 11, maybe 12 days. I can't remember the date when I stopped, and when I was moved over to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I can't specify, really, how many months, but I, I went to work in kitchen -- in the kitchen for four times, and four times I left the kitchen; that is, sometimes for a month, sometimes for two months, and I would be off and then would come again. It could have been about, well, during a period of ten months, I think, but I'm not really a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: During my first round there, there were six of us, quite a number of prisoners, and they needed people to wash dishes, distribute food, slice bread, and we were doing it there under the supervision of civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the civilian police. Were you also supervised by the cooks, professional cooks?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, they were responsible for us who worked in the kitchen. We were under their control, the civilian cook, who used to work there before the war. They ran the kitchen, and we were under their supervision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, you discussed serving food to the prison staff. Did there come a time when the prison staff stopped eating on the KP Dom premises and started eating somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It was after quite some time, perhaps a couple of months later, a separate restaurant was opened outside the compound, which existed even before the war, for both the employees and for outsiders. And I suppose somebody suggested that it be open again, either by the warden or somebody else, so that they could take their meals there, so that they were not coming to the compound to take their meals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that was, when the outside restaurant opened?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I am not sure. It could have been seven or eight months after the outbreak of the war it could have been done. Yes, I should say seven or eight months, but I'm not sure, to be quite honest. I wasn't really -- all that I was concerned about was how to survive. I didn't really pay much attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also before the break you mentioned that the prison staff and the detainees had their food in different pots. Could you tell us the difference in quality and quantity of the food that the prison staff received and that the detainees received?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. If you are asking about inmates, like we were, I mean, there were some Serb prisoners who were there because of some transgressions. There was also a big difference. And if you mean the staff and the guards who had their meals in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. compound, the difference was even greater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start with a description of the food that the staff and the guards received. What kind of food did they have available to them?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, their food was quite wholesome. They could have what they wanted: eggs different ways, meat, tins. They could have anything they liked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the Serb prisoners who were there. What kind of food and how much could they have?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: They also did not eat bad; not as good as the guards or the staff, but they had decent food. The boss told me personally, "Well, give them as much bread as they want or whatever they ask, give it to them," so we had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did the Muslim detainees receive to eat?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, it was rather critical for a while. Bread was sliced into 11 slices; and for a month or two or so began to cut it into 10 slices; and then later on it improved slightly and it was cut into 9 slices. So those were really thin slices. There were very many of us and I really sliced tonnes of that bread. And that was that. And some soup. Allegedly they had nothing else. Practically it was little more than water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many slices of bread was each Muslim detainee allowed per day?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Per day, you mean? Well, in the morning you go to have your breakfast and then your supper, lunch; a slice of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you received three meals a day and each meal you received one slice of bread; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes. That was the ration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve the bread to the detainees as they came in?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I did. Not all the time, because we took shifts. Some -- one of us slices it, some distributes bread, some pours out or, rather, ladles out soup.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you or the people serving the Muslim detainees allowed to give more than one slice of bread to each detainee?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No. We were told, we were warned, cautioned specifically to take care, to mind not to give anyone more bread. And I heard very many criticisms from other Muslims that I hadn't given them enough bread, and they would look around and say that there was so much bread around me. But, you know, I stand there, they are behind me, other people, and I did not give anyone any more bread even though they're quite famished, they can barely walk, and yet I did not dare give them more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told what would happen to you if you dared give more than a slice of bread to a hungry detainee?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, yes. At least seven days of solitary confinement and then you can't work there again, or then you are hit, you are struck with a baton, and it would never occur to you again to give anyone an extra slice of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there guards present to make sure, to enforce this rule?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes. When a column goes for breakfast or lunch, then there's a guard in front and a guard behind. And if he's not in front of the line, then he comes with the head cook, chief cook, and stands with him and watches how the food is distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there also measures to prevent you and other people working in the kitchen, other detainees, from taking food out of the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: At the end, that is, for instance, in the evening, when I would finish my job, the guard would come to take me to my room. Before that, he searches me in detail to see if I had stolen something, a piece of bread or something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever mistreated during these searches?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, but not many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you. It is difficult to talk about those people who stooped so low. I can mention Vukovic, who on a couple of occasions gave me a scare and kicked me in the - pardon the expression - in the arse or perhaps slapped me in the face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the first name of this Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. Allegedly he -- I don't know exactly what his name is, but allegedly he harmed some people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a guard at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you any reason why he was slapping or kicking you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, once he said to me -- I didn't really know him well, and once he said that he knew me well, which I know, and then he did that, which he shouldn't have done, but, well ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the incident or group of incidents described here is listed in Schedule A, incident number 13. There is a first name provided of that guard and the last name is the same, and the guard whom we believe this is referring to is also listed in the exhibit P3 at number 52.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also bring food to detainees who were kept in solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Some, yes, but not very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember specifically any detainee who was kept in solitary confinement to whom you brought food?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the name or names of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Rasim Kiselica, a tradesman from Godinje who was taken to solitary confinement, from Godinje, and I was the first one to take him lunch or supper or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: There were some whom I could not see. I could recognise Rasim well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why these people were put in solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I couldn't say. Allegedly, Rasim and his women are (redacted) now. He said that they found him at home, put him in a car, brought him to the KP Dom and in solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it that you had to bring them food? Were they allowed to go to the canteen to get food with everyone else?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Oh, come, no. Solitary confinement is solitary confinement. Before the war and, of course, the state of war, you can't even see him, let alone let him into some other room. Well, I managed to take some food to him and to see him, but they were not allowed to come out or get food or some -- anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your bringing food to them was in your official capacity as part of your kitchen work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, but it all depended on guards. If a guard sees that one of them cannot do it, then he finds one of the inmates working in the kitchen and tells him to take this food. You go to the door, the guard opens the door, give this food to the guard, and the guard just throws it in. Well, as an isolation cell, like an isolation cell, like an isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of your kitchen work, did you also have to get fuel to operate the stove?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: There was no fuel, and the power was cut off and there was no steam, because they were all steam-operated stoves. And we had to make a kitchen stove in the yard where we cooked meals for inmates. And in the morning I had to chop wood and then light the fire in the morning so that when the head cook came, everything would be ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time when you had to go outside the KP Dom to the river to get wood?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I did that two or three times, thanks to a nice guard who allowed me to go to the Drina and to take some dry branches fallen off poplars, and I used that to light the fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time when you had to use the wooden pillars of a destroyed mosque to light the stove?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I twice seized that opportunity. I found two or three pillars, and my guess was that they came from Careva dzamija because that was pine wood. And although that is a shame, a sin, a disgrace, yet nevertheless I chopped those because -- and I kept that as firewood to help me light the fire in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you find those pillars?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It was across the KP Dom town where cars are parked next to -- on the Drina bank, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were the pillars there? Were they arranged in any way, or did they look like they had just been dumped there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, I suppose a lorry must have brought that and then unloaded it. There were some other structural construction material. I didn't pay much attention to that. I saw those two or three pillars, and I decided to chop them and use them then as firewood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually recognise those pillars as coming from the Careva mosque?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I did, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the Careva mosque located? Was it also in Foca?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It was in Foca, above the green market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever required to give a statement at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: For two or three months, I kept trying to get to the warden and make a statement, and the last time I asked for that, a guard came and said, "Taranin, wait. You're asking for too much. Your time will come." So that I just stopped trying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you trying to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, I thought that I was a man who had nothing negative about him. I lived well with everyone, including the Serbs. I was an honest citizen. I thought that I would be interviewed, interrogated, and that then they would release me. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you eventually taken to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: On one occasion as I was working in the kitchen, Krsto Krnojelac came and said, "Taranin, come to the gate. A guard is waiting for you to give a statement." Since I wore a white uniform, because cooks and kitchen helpers had to have white kitchen uniforms, and he said, "Never mind, just take off your cap," and that's what I did. And then the guard met me there and said come on to this room in a hall which was pretty long, about 20 or 30 metres. That's where I found three or four men, prisoners. I didn't really look at them very carefully, and I couldn't recognise who they were, and the guard said, "You line up here with them." That's what I did. After two or three minutes, not more than that, three inspectors showed up, Starovic Slobo was the first one, and Koprivica, and the third one who worked in the crime prevention service before as well. I'll give you his name, I just forgot it right now. Vladicic, Vladicic, that was the third one. Vladicic said to me -- or rather, he said to his colleagues, "Who will take Taranin over?" Koprivica immediately said that he would. He said, "Let Rasim come with me." He took me by the arm and brought me into a room. He followed me into that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you went into the room with him? What kinds of things did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: He said, "Sit down." He took off his coat. He took out his briefcase. He looked at some papers two or three times. He took a pack of cigarettes, put it in front of him. He opened that pack. He offered me a cigarette. I refused, I didn't want to smoke, and he said, "Don't be frightened. Take a cigarette. Light up." And I took that cigarette. He lit it. He lit my cigarette, too, as well as his own. We both smoked a cigarette. He said to me that he knew me and he asked me whether I knew him. I could not remember at first, but later on I did remember him, because his brother played soccer well. He followed sports too. And I was also in sports organisations. I was there all the time. So we both smoked a cigarette and we didn't talk about anything really except for such private matters. Finally he said to me, "I see that you're frightened. Don't be frightened. You're a good man. Let me just ask you one thing: What is Emir Taranin to you? Who is he?" And he [as interpreted] said, "He's my brother's son. He's about 16 years old." "Did he have any weapons?" I said that I never saw him with a weapon. And then he said, "Some people say that they saw him with a weapon." And I said, "Believe me, I don't. On Saturdays and Sundays I worked as well. I mean, he could have had an automatic rifle, but I really didn't know about that. Actually, we were not on very good terms, this brother of mine and I, and we did have this house but we are not on very good terms, so I didn't really check on him, what he was doing and who had what." And then this man said, "Rasim, we trust you. We know you as a citizen. We'll have another cigarette." And then he said, "You're going to sign this record." I didn't even see him write all of that and all this, and then he said, "I can read this out to you." And then I said, "Oh, I trust you. You don't have to read it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'll sign it." And that's exactly the way we did it. I mean, nobody believed me that I did so well with the inspectors, that I fared so well with this inspector, and I want to thank him on this occasion as well for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether other detainees were beaten while they were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: There were all sorts of things. I could not see that. Some listened to that, but I didn't even try to listen and I couldn't see it, because when a man is frightened, he's not really up to that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you frightened of hearing?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: You know, when you hear somebody beating somebody else and when you hear this other person moaning and crying, then you have the feeling that you're going to be next. And this feeling goes through your entire body and, begging your pardon, you may even piss in your pants out of fear. It's so bad when you get into a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually hear the sounds of people being beaten if you didn't cover your ears?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Some listened. I couldn't listen. I didn't dare try do that. This usually happened in the night shift, when they would come in the evening at 7.00. They took people out for interrogations and there were these really negative situations. Some people had the patience to listen to all these screams and moans. In the evening, as soon as I would finish, I would lie down, I would cover myself, and I would wait. I would wait to see what my fate would be and I could hardly wait for the break of dawn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you name some of the detainees who were beaten in this way?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: They say there were quite a few. I did not see them. I saw Nurko Nisic when he came to the kitchen. He was seriously injured in the face, all blue. I saw him when he was lined up there. He was beaten up very badly. Perhaps there were others too, but I did not notice all of that, but I noticed that Nurko was all blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, this Nurko Nisic is listed on Schedule C at number 19.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of anyone else that you saw beaten or saw injuries as a result of beatings?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say. I have to tell the truth here. If somebody were beaten very badly, then it would be very hard for him to show up where the other prisoners were. They would not line up with the rest of the prisoners. I mean, people would be terrified if they were to see that, so perhaps they would throw them into isolation cells or something, or I don't know. There weren't any exchanges or things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you saw him with the injuries, was he by himself or with a group of other detainees?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: He was in a group with other detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you made the comment that there weren't any exchanges or anything like that. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I mean all those groups that went out. They said that they were all going out for an exchange, and we were all pleased, and we all tried to get into these groups, to get into those exchanges. And when I got out, my phone wouldn't stop ringing. People kept asking me where these people were. There were women calling me and asking about their husbands and other people, and everybody was asking. The only thing I could say was, "He went out for an exchange," and see, they're missing until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe how these people were taken out, the ones that you said were told they would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, a guard would get into a room where there was a man who was supposed to go out, and then say -- he'd say, "Taranin, you're going out and you're supposed to make a statement." That's how people were taken out. And those who were not afraid would sometimes look through the window and then they would usually gather them in front of the gate. Five or ten or whoever, the number of prisoners that were supposed to be taken out, they would go to the gate, and then -- and then they would interrogate them in their own way, the way they know how to do this. I don't know. Those who listened, they heard moans and cries and - I don't know - things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were taken out in the way that you've described, did you see them returned to the rooms?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Some were returned and some were taken to isolation cells, and I could not see all of this. I mean, you had to follow it in order to know. I never dared go to the window to see. I don't know. It's not only me, that I didn't dare watch this; many didn't dare watch this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there also people taken out in this way who were not returned to the rooms or isolation cells whom you didn't see again at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: There were such cases. That's what people say, people who watched. I really did not follow this. I couldn't see it. But there was quite a bit of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you worked in the kitchen, did you have another work assignment?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: After that, I was told to go to the workshop because I'm a mechanic. That is my basic craft. That is what I originally trained for. So I was sent to the workshop. And there seemed to have been a bare minimum in the kitchen, so some Serbs were brought in. Only I and Ismir Hadic [phoen] remained in the kitchen. He was sent to the laundry from there and I was sent to the workshop to help his father, Hamdo, who worked in the workshop before that. And then there was also this man called Sefko Kubat there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, Sefko Kubat is mentioned at Schedule E, number 37.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do in the mechanic's workshop?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: All the cars that were there, primarily these special trucks for transporting furniture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: We maintained these vehicles, mechanics, tyres, everything. All three of us worked on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this workshop inside the KP Dom premises or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It's not within the compound where we were; it's in another compound. That was also closed. This was a special workshop that had a mechanical shop, a locksmith shop, and also a lathe shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to get to that workshop, did you have to go outside the KP Dom gate?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: We had to go outside the main gate. We would be lined up one by one, and as we were to go out, we were all checked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who put you on this work assignment; do you know?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
