utterances.text: As far as I know, this assignment was worked out by Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever paid for the work that you did as a mechanic while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, if I can say so. They gave me an extra slice of bread and sometimes they would spread something on that slice of bread. This was an additional bonus for those who worked in the mechanic's workshop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you choose to be part of the mechanics workshop?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: There was no choice. It depended on the assignment, where they assigned you to. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the same true for your work in the kitchen, that you had no choice?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: How can I make my own choice when I'm in a camp? When I'm told to do something, I have to do it, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you worked in the kitchen, did you receive extra food?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I didn't. I tried to be impartial. I tried to steal something if my head cook or my policeman would not be watching and would not see me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I succeeded several times to soak a slice of bread into hot water, and then when nobody was watching, to eat up that slice of bread, hot and moist, real fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose weight while you were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: About 18 or 19 kilos. I'm not sure that's how much I lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were working at the mechanics workshop, did anyone try to escape from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe who that was and what the consequences were?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Enes, whose last name was -- I'll remember the last name. He was a locksmith. He works -- he worked at the locksmith shop; that is to say, within the same compound where I was but in a different department. He managed to -- because in that compound everything was destroyed on the site facing the main road, so it later turned out that around 2.00 he managed to get out and simply pass by as the group of civilians who were getting out of the hospital and all that, and then he managed to reach the neighbourhood of Brod, and then that's where he stayed. And then the next day he wanted to proceed, but that's where they caught up with him and brought him back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the rest of you in the mechanics workshop when it was discovered that he had escaped?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Bad problems. It was hard to survive then. There was a lot of pressure brought to bear on us. None of us knew that he would try to escape. When we went to lunch, we realised that Enes was not there, and then they asked us, Savo Todovic asked us, "Where is he?" We didn't know. He asked some guards. They didn't know either. We went to have lunch, and from there we went to the room where we slept. Savo Todovic ordered that we all go back to in front of the gate, and the policeman returned all of us to the gate. And when we got to the gate, Savo Todovic was there, waiting for us. He wore weapons. He carried weapons. He had an automatic rifle, and he said, "Whoever does not say who Enes is, whoever does not say where Enes escaped will be killed." And he swore -- he said that he had two sons. I don't know until this very day whether he really has two sons or not. He swore by his sons that he would kill all of us in two or three minutes if they did not -- if they did not tell him, that they would be killed. And we were all looking at each other and yelling, "Whoever knows should speak up." But nobody really knew. We were so lucky, at least that's the way I see it. Boro Ivanovic came and he said, "Savo, what's going on?" And he said, "Well, one of them escaped." "Which one?" And they said the name. And he said that we should all go to the metal shop. We all went to the metal shop, and we were lined up against a wall, and we were supposed to say where he escaped and how and when. First Ivanovic asked me. And Ivanovic said to me, "Taranin, I know you as a man, as a colleague, a huntsman. Be honest and say where he is." I answered him, I swear by my own child that I did not know where he was. I can say that until the present day. I did not know. I swear I did not know. Then he asked a few others, and they did not know, and then said that we should go to the room where we slept. That's exactly what we did. We all went to the room. However, Savo ordered all of us to go to the solitary confinement cells, and that's exactly what happened. About nine of us were placed in one isolation cell. And he said he would come later to interrogate us so that we would say where he was, and if we were not to say where he was, we would be tried. Well, we were tried, indeed. Somebody got 20 days, somebody got a month, somebody got even more than that in solitary confinement. The next day, luckily, they found him. They brought him in. We didn't know about this. We did stand trial, and I got 25 days of solitary confinement. After three days, they took us out of the solitary confinement cell. We didn't know that they had found him. We were up there, in front of the kitchen, on a plateau. He was standing there. Warden Krnojelac, Mico, was there, too. Savo Todovic was there. The commander of the guards, Rasevic, and another guard was there, I can't remember which one. Todovic said to me, "Taranin, get out." And I got out of the line. He said, "Do you know Zekovic, your friend?" I said "Yes, I know him." And then he said, "And you didn't know that he'd escaped?" And I tell you until this day, I did not know. Here is the gentleman, he himself, he can say whether I knew. And he said, "No one knew. When I want to do something like that, I don't tell anyone." I wanted to tell him another thing, and he wouldn't allow me to. He said, "Taranin, there's nothing for you to say. Go back into the line." And then he said, "Don't try to escape. Nobody can escape from here. Not even a bird can get out of this Serb state." And then he took us back to the isolation cell, and he threatened that he would cut our existing food rations by 50 per cent. I had great luck in managing to survive six days in this solitary confinement cell. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was sent out. I was exchanged. I was sent to Rudo so that I would proceed to Gorazde. And that morning I was taken out of solitary confinement. I was taken to the gate, and they said that I would be going to Rudo for an exchange, which is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo, during the course of that very long answer, the witness said that he had been asked by, I think, Todovic, "You know Zekovic." Now, is that the person -- is that the name that he was thinking of before? He's been referring to this person who escaped as Enes. It may be necessary to link them up so it's not confused with the Enes on Schedule C.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, that's a good point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Zekovic the name of the person who escaped?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Enes Zekovic. Thank you. Yes, that's right, Enes Zekovic. I know his father, too. I know his entire family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were placed in the solitary confinement cell, you said there were nine of you in one cell. Were you able to sit down or lie down in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No. It was impossible to lie down or to sit because an isolation cell -- I don't know whether all of you know about this, an isolation is an isolation cell. It is small, narrow. It's for one person, and nine of us were thrown in there, and it was impossible to sit or to lie down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, if you could -- if you could sleep while you were standing, then you slept, but you can't sleep when you're so afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you were in solitary confinement for six days. Were all nine of you in the same cell for six days?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Until I left, all of us were in the same isolation cell. They stayed after me. I don't know when they got out, but thanks to this bit of luck, I managed to get out on the sixth day, so I did not spend all the 25 days that I was supposed to spend there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody was beaten as a result of the escape of Mr. Zekovic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: When I was in the isolation cell, Todovic came with a guard. I could not see him. I could not recognise his voice, either. I was in an isolation cell. Savo asked one of them there, I think his name was Lija. He also worked in a servicing station before. He asked him who his best friend was, and as far as I could hear, somebody slapped that Lija in the face so that he would say who he was. He said that I was his good friend, and that I played cards with him, that I played gin rummy with him, and that I would know best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With whom? Whose best friend?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Enes Zekovic, because it was all before they had -- before they caught him. It was then that Todovic came with a guard to interrogate at the other end of the corridor where solitary confinement are, where Lija was kept - his surname was Lisica - and then they questioned him separately there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: For the Court's cross reference, the incident that has been described with the escaped detainee is in the indictment at paragraph 5.21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After six days in solitary confinement, you said you were taken to Rudo. How was it that you were taken there? How did that come about? Who took you there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: On the sixth day of my confinement, around nine or ten in the morning, in the corridor one could hear a voice asking, "Where is Taranin?" And the guard who was with him said, "In this cell here." I don't know which number that cell had. I do not know to this day. And then he said, "Well, let him out." And he opened the door and said, "Taranin, come out." There was Prodanovic, an inspector. That is what we called him, the man who used to work for the KP Dom before. And he said, "Taranin, have you got any belongings with you? In ten minutes, be at the gate." And I said I had a few things, I think a coat, a pair of socks. "May I take that?" He said, "Yes, and be downstairs in ten minutes." So I hurried. I didn't know where I was going, or why I was going. And when I reached the gate, that Prodanovic was downstairs. And downstairs I found quite a number of people. There were about 17 of us when I counted us later on. We were all lined up, and they began to check various people, to search various people, and I was one of them. And Prodanovic frisked me and let me through the gate, and we lined up in front of the gate. And then an army van came up and with three policemen and two civilians. One of them was a driver, and another one was, I guess, a mechanic, and the rest were armed, some kind of military police. So Todovic called out our names, and as our names would be called out, we boarded the van. And when we were in the van, one of those guards also came up and said, "Pull all the curtains. Don't you dare watch, and just you may look only ahead." And he got off, and then Todovic came up, and then another guard came who perhaps was the head guard and called out our names and we responded. And after that we set off through Celebici, Tuzla, Pljevlja, and thus reached Rudo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being taken to Rudo?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I learnt when I left, and it was Prodanovic who told me that, "Well, good luck to you. You're going to Rudo to be exchanged, and then on to Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so for the Court's benefit, where is Rudo located in reference to Foca, in which direction and how far?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It is towards the east, towards Serbia. It is about 120, 130 kilometres from Foca. You go towards Gorazde, then you turn towards Visegrad, across Bijele Brdo towards Turbats [phoen] which separates Priboj from Rudo, or you take another road before Visegrad to Medzedza, or rather, before Medzedza to the right up the Lim river, and that is how you can also reach Rudo. So it's somewhere close to the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in Rudo were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I knew Rudo from before, so I recognised the place when we arrived there. They took us to the cultural centre and put us in the cellar there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in that cellar?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly, but I should say that we spent not less than eight or nine months in Rudo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody in the cellar when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No. There was nobody there. It was quite empty. But before us somebody had been there. Whether Serbs or Muslims, I don't know, but one could see some cardboard boxes and one could see traces of blood on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your group of 17 were brought there, was anyone else brought to join you?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes. The first one was Durmo, a man of 83, who reportedly, about a month before we arrived there, had surrendered to the Rudo authorities and who was kept in the barracks. But when we arrived, he was brought over to that same cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else join you there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes. When they -- when we were told that we would be exchanged - however, it somehow couldn't be pulled off because of our authorities or somebody else - they would not take us as civilians in exchange for some combatants from Rudo who had been captured. And then we were joined by two men from Gorazde who had been caught somewhere at Grebak and another man who was -- and Sefko, who was 60 something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned civilians. Were the whole group of you from KP Dom civilians?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: All those that I mentioned so far were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to leave the cellar in Rudo?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Not for a while, but that did not last long. Presumably their chief - I don't know his name. I forgot what he was called - but I heard he used to be a professional guard in the central prison in Sarajevo and that he had been assigned as our warden. And as far as we could say, he was quite decent. He did not keep us there long. He told us to come out, to do something, to sweep the streets in the town, to remove the garbage, and then sent us to pick fruit - apples, plums - to go to the barracks to do something, so that we managed to be active, to come out into the air, to do something with ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You called the person in charge of this place in Rudo a warden. Did you regard your situation in Rudo as being in another prison camp or detention centre?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, how shall I put it? That was the situation that we were in. The accommodation was worse than in Foca, but on the other hand, the food was much better and we could go out. And it happened to be at a time when there was plenty of fruit around. So as I've said, the accommodation was much worse in Rudo, but on the other hand, the food was much better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the warden ever take action against anybody who mistreated you at Rudo?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, rather pretty decent; I have to say that. There were some attempts, perhaps by some civilians, who would sometimes try to do something, but owing to those, we survived. It was all right, even though there were some incidents. Well, I can tell you about the incident that I experienced. It was one day in the barracks when they had assigned some of us to remove some machines that were standing in front of some administrative building because General Pero Skopljak was allegedly coming, so that we should clear the area, make some order. And we went to do that and we were finishing the job when a group of soldiers turned up, and one of them came to me and said, "Well, how is it?" And I said, "It's all right." And when I said that I'm fine, then he kicked me with his shoe on the right-hand side twice. And when he kicked me the second time, I lost air and I fell. And two minutes later, he hit another one in the face, in the eye, but they then carried me to the kitchen and I came to and they gave me some tea or something and took me to where we were accommodated. And the next day they took me to see a doctor, and he found that I had three broken ribs. And they gave me a sick leave of some 14, 15 days to recover. I didn't have to work or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they" carried you out and gave you tea, who was that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, those were some of mine, that is, one of the guards who had escorted us, called Ivanovic, from Strpci. And I guess another one of those soldiers helped him to carry me, and one of those folk of mine, such as Isakovic and some others. So that when I came to, I was in the kitchen. I didn't know what had happened. I felt pain on the left-hand side. I couldn't really touch it. So that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the person you described as the warden at Rudo come speak to you about the incident, tell you anything about whether it would happen again in the future?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: He came; at least, that's what guard Ivanovic told us. He told not only me, everybody, "Taranin, I don't think this will happen again. And if we see that there's any danger, then you will not go there," and he will tell the commander to remove such man from those positions, because the warden won't give any more men to help out if such things happen again. So I can only thank him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the nine months or so in Rudo, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: For about two days I worked in that army workshop. They asked me to try to repair a vehicle, and they had on old mechanic and we succeeded in doing that. And then a policeman came in a van and asked to take me somewhere. I got scared, and this man said, "Why are you taking him?" And he said, "Well, I need Taranin." And I said, "Well, I am not Taranin." But he said, "You are being exchanged." Then I said, "Yes, right, so that's me." And they took me up there and I saw some 10 or 15 men of them and they all had bags over their shoulders because they were getting ready for exchange. And I said, "So where are you taking us?" And he said, "To Sarajevo." We were all happy and we were all merry, and two vans arrived, so they put us onto those vans in the afternoon to take us to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: They took us to Kula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It's a prison. It was a prison before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it located?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It is near Sarajevo, or rather quite close to the airport. There was a restaurant, Kula. There was a prison there and they had a building unit there, but it was a large prison. It was mostly a prison for minor offences, for misdemeanours before the war, and that is where they put us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept at the Kula prison camp?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you exactly, but it was a couple of months or so. So sometime on the 6th or 7th of October I left that camp, at a time of a major exchange of about four or five hundred people. They had brought civilians from Rogatica, and I suppose it was thanks to them that we were exchanged. We were three or four hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: 1994. Let me think. 6th or 7th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of the time that you spent at the KP Dom prison camp, what physical effects did you suffer?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I fared very badly, as shown by the state of my health, which I cannot even describe you. It would be the medical commissioner, people who treated me for years after I came out, could describe it much better than I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there -- how did you suffer emotionally or psychologically?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Very severe. There was a doctor, specialist, who said quite openly that they were very happy to rehabilitate me psychologically. They tried to send me to a school, but I simply couldn't remember. My memory failed me. I still cannot speak any (redacted). And I was a mechanic. I knew all those things and I tried to learn that terminology in (redacted), but I cannot do it. And the doctor said, "Well, we're happy that we managed to rehabilitate you and help you to communicate with the (redacted) at least something, but you cannot go back." I'm still suffering consequences. A couple of years ago I suffered a stroke and they barely managed to pull me out. But I am retired now. They gave me a pension because I'm unable to communicate properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time when you were suicidal?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: In the early days, yes, quite often you think about it: Kill yourself, kill yourself. But, well, one never stops hoping. And I managed to live, and I cannot but thank those who helped me live, find my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Those are all the questions we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think I will be very brief and I will do my best to finish by 4.00. Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Taranin, I see that you are upset, so if you want a break, if you need some time to recover, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: No, no, no. Go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I am one of the counsel of the accused Krnojelac and my name is Mihajlo Bakrac. Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall be very brief. I merely want to clarify a couple of things, nothing more than that. A moment ago when my learned friend asked you about your departure from the KP Dom to Rudo, you said then that when you were in front of the gate there were three military policemen and that Todovic then read out the names from the list. All I want is to clarify. When you say "Todovic," do you mean Savo Todovic?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: That's right, Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend also helped me when she asked you about the statement that you made to the OTP investigators, to whom you said that Mr. Krnojelac was a warden on paper, and you explained what you meant by that. I want to ask you an additional question with reference to the same statement. Is it true that when you spoke about the working group, that you said that it was set up by Savo Todovic, who commanded us and other staff in the KP Dom? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in that same statement, referring to Velibor Ostojic and Vojislav Maksimovic, you said, "In my view," that is, that in your view, those two were the principal culprits because they held leading political offices, and that it was by no accident that Todovic, who was -- that Todovic, who was Ostojic's relative, and that that was how he was assigned to a high post in the KP Dom? I know that they come from the same village, from Celebici.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I don't know if they are related, but I know they come from the same place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us if it is true what I read out to you.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Well, the whole Europe, not only we, know that he was one of the leading Serbs, one of the leading -- one of the political leaders of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Bakrac, I think the interpreter is about three questions behind you. I know you're trying to hurry to finish it this afternoon, but I think it's best to take it slowly. If necessary, we come back in the morning. But you are not giving the interpreters any chance at all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm really trying to save time and expenses, not to have the witness back tomorrow for just -- because of one or two questions. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand, but it's more important that we get it down properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I agree, and it is also in the interests of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall repeat: Is it true that you said -- I read a long sentence to you so as to keep it within the context, but the gist of it is that you said that it was by no accident that Todovic, who was Ostojic's relative, was given a high post in the KP Dom? Because I know that they both come from the same village of Celebici.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: They come -- it is possible that they come from the same village and that he was probably assigned by him, because Savo Todovic used to work for the KP Dom before, so that was the duty that he had that. He already worked in the KP Dom, so it does not mean -- it doesn't have to mean that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in your statement given to the state Security Centre in Sarajevo on the 25th of October, 1994, you said: "The prison warden was Krnojelac, his deputy Todovic, and he was -- he had the main say in everything. He was responsible for accommodation, for assignment of jobs, for harassment of people. He was the one who had the last say"?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so. Perhaps you interpreted it wrongly or read it -- or misread it. I wouldn't say so. Krnojelac was the warden of the prison and his first name was -- I forget it. No. Mico. That's what all the Focas called him: Mico. His deputy was Todovic, who used to work there before. Of the inner compound, it was Todovic, as can be seen from all the statements, including mine. He, yes, he assigned people. Whether he did on his own or whether he received some guidelines from the warden, I do not know that, but in the compound he did that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is whether you stated this to the public Security Centre, and is this your signature? And I shall now ask the usher to show you the statement that you gave to a person who speaks the same language as you do and if this signature on that document is yours.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Where is that sentence? Let me see. I want to see what it says here. Where is that sentence? The signature is mine; I agree with that. But I'm telling you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just both of you stop. Just stop. You are both speaking over each other and the translators are having great difficulties. Now, if you are going to keep up this speed, we'll just adjourn. Please do keep down the rate of questions. Wait for the answer, wait for the translators to finish the translation. Now, Mr. Taranin, you said that it was your signature, but -- and you were going to add something. What was it that you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I said that Krnojelac was the warden of the prison, that his deputy was Savo Todovic, that everything that -- that all the jobs inside were performed by Todovic, whether he received any guidelines from Krnojelac or not, but he was the one who assigned duties and all the rest, and that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness wanted to read, and I insist that he read the sentence in the 27th line from the word "statement," and it begins with the words, "The warden of the prison was Krnojelac." I want him to read out that sentence. Perhaps I could show the usher where the sentence begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why don't you read it out to him and ask him if he agrees that that's in the statement. It would be much quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, I shall read it verbatim as the statement says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The prison warden was Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the deputy Todovic who was number one for everything, for accommodation, assignment of jobs, and harassment of people, his opinion was invited in everything?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean this is correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned today the incident with Mr. Zekovic's escape. You also mentioned somebody called Boro Ivanovic. Will you please explain who was Boro Ivanovic, and what was his duty, if you know it.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: I do not know what he was because I wasn't a part of their circle, so I don't know that. But I know Boro Ivanovic as a civilian, as a hunter, as a colleague. I do not know what rank he had, but I heard that he was a security Major. However, that need not be true. That is only what I heard. But he saved us because, otherwise, there might have been some consequences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you mentioned ranks, so you mean he was part of the military structure?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came to the KP Dom the first time, did you know that there were some Serb inmates there, serving their terms following judgements?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Before the war, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, did you find some of those individuals in the KP Dom when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes, three. One was very sick, and two more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what you knew about them?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN
utterances.text: Yes. There were three of them. There was nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have three, four, maybe five questions more. It is 4.00. It is up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think that you have given the translators a hard enough time already. We'll adjourn now till 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of January, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.
